title: Infinity War's Fake Hulk Trailer Shot Raises Questions About Doomsday
excerpt:
An iconic Wakanda charge in Infinity War's marketing never appeared in the finished movie.
The example is fueling fresh caution about interpreting Avengers: Doomsday trailers.
body_md:
Marketing for major Marvel crossovers can be as carefully engineered as the movies themselves. As excitement builds around Avengers: Doomsday, a retrospective looks at one of the most memorable examples of a promotional shot that did not represent the finished film: the Wakanda charge in the Avengers: Infinity War trailer.

The 2018 promotional footage showed Captain America, Black Panther, Hulk and other heroes running toward the camera together. It looked like a defining image of the climactic battle. In the released film, however, that particular formation never appears. Bruce Banner cannot bring Hulk out during the Wakanda sequence and instead fights inside the Hulkbuster armor.

The Russo brothers later confirmed that the hero shot was created for marketing. That distinction matters: this was not merely a scene accidentally lost during the final edit. The trailer also featured a memorable Thanos line about the balance of the universe that was replaced before release. These changes became lasting examples of how Marvel can alter what viewers think they know.

There is a practical reason for the approach. Large franchise movies need extensive promotional campaigns, yet revealing too much authentic footage can spoil surprise appearances and narrative turns. Concealing a character, changing a background or manufacturing a shot can preserve the theatrical experience. At the same time, such decisions can frustrate viewers who expect a spectacular trailer moment to appear in the movie they paid to see.

The new commentary applies that history to material associated with Doomsday. It discusses purported footage involving Avengers and X-Men, Thor and Doctor Doom, Sentinels and multiversal incursions. The central question is not whether every reported image is false, but whether audiences should treat any individual promotional shot as definitive evidence of the finished plot.

No particular Doomsday shot is proven fake by this argument. The article offers a comparison and a warning rather than verified behind-the-scenes information about alterations to the upcoming film. A scene may survive unchanged, be digitally modified or exist only as part of a campaign; viewers cannot reliably distinguish those possibilities from a trailer alone.

Marvel faces an unusually delicate marketing challenge as it approaches the conclusion of its current multiverse storyline. It must generate excitement among longtime fans while protecting surprises big enough to justify a theatrical event. The real test of the campaign's honesty and effectiveness will come when the finished movie can be compared with its promotional footage.
